author: goldturtle
body:
@marcfeuermann @pgaudet: submitted with the PAINT issue template's fields. The posting account cannot set labels, so please add `PAINT annotation`.

* **PTHR ID & PTN node:** PTHR10603; PTN001318100 (gain of positive regulation of translation, GO:0045727); PTN001318100 (v1 gain of negative regulation of translation, GO:0017148; dropped)

* **Sequences with problematic annotation (ID + gene/protein name):** UniProtKB:Q06787 FMR1 (fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1)

* **Type of Issue:** Other: the gain of negative regulation of translation was dropped since v1.

*How this draft was made:* an automated screen compared every PAN-GO (IBA) annotation of human genes (release 2025-10-12_2.0.5, PANTHER 19) with the genes' experimental annotations in GO release 2025-10-10. Flagged annotations were then judged by evidence-cited reasoning (Claude subagents, citing only a curated evidence pack). The statements below were checked against the GO, PAN-GO and PANTHER data, and the papers behind the key annotations were read. Please treat it as a candidate for curator review.


**Inherited:** FMR1 `involved_in` *positive regulation of translation* ([GO:0045727](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0045727))

- **Gain:** PTN001318100 (speciation, Metazoa-Choanoflagellida; human genes below: FMR1, FXR1, FXR2), dated 2023-04-05.
- **Evidence genes (5):** Fmr1 (DROME), Fxr1 (MOUSE), Fmr1 (MOUSE), FXR1 (HUMAN), FMR1 (HUMAN).
- **Relation to FMR1:** includes FMR1 itself; orthologs: Fmr1 (DROME), Fmr1 (MOUSE); paralogs: Fxr1 (MOUSE), FXR1 (HUMAN).
- **Other human genes inheriting it:** FXR1, FXR2.
- **Losses of this term in the family:** none.
- **v1 (paper release):** same annotation, from PTN001318100.

**Dropped since v1:** *negative regulation of translation* ([GO:0017148](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0017148)), gained at PTN001318100 (dated 2020-09-29). The node is still in the current tree; the gain was removed.

**FMR1's own experimental annotations** (GO release 2025-10-10) for the dropped term:

- *translation repressor activity* ([GO:0030371](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0030371)): [PMID:11157796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11157796/) (IDA)
- *negative regulation of translation* ([GO:0017148](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0017148)): [PMID:12417522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12417522/) (IDA), [PMID:30765518](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30765518/) (IDA), [PMID:31439799](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31439799/) (IDA)

**FMR1's own experimental annotations** (GO release 2025-10-10) against *positive regulation of translation*: 3 opposing, 2 supporting:

- *negative regulation of translation* ([GO:0017148](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0017148)): [PMID:12417522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12417522/) (IDA), [PMID:30765518](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30765518/) (IDA), [PMID:31439799](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31439799/) (IDA)

**Literature (Textpresso, all species corpora):** 46 sentences mention FMR1 together with *translation*. By cue words, 14 describe the opposite of the inherited direction and 6 agree.

> **FUS and FMRP repress translation in vitro Biomolecular condensates are thought to antagonize translation (25, 26), and FMRP phase separation correlates with translation inhibition (23).**

— Birsa N, Ule AM, Garone MG, Tsang B, Mattedi F, Chong PA et al. (2021). FUS-ALS mutants alter FMRP phase separation equilibrium and impair protein translation. *Science advances*. [PMID:34290090](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34290090/).


> FMRP inhibits translation through several mechanisms, including polysome binding, miRNA and RNA-induced silencing complex–dependent repression, or binding to translation initiation factors (43). **More recently, FMRP LLPS has been shown to correlate with translation inhibition in vitro (23), and in vivo FMRP granule formation decreases the translation of FMRP-bound synaptic targets (50).** This adds complexity to the FMRP-dependent regulation of translation and supports a model in which an increase in FMRP condensates could be associated with decreased translation of FMRP targets.

— Birsa N, Ule AM, Garone MG, Tsang B, Mattedi F, Chong PA et al. (2021). FUS-ALS mutants alter FMRP phase separation equilibrium and impair protein translation. *Science advances*. [PMID:34290090](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34290090/).


**Sentences counted as agreeing** (6): one supports it. A 2022 study found many large proteins translationally reduced without FMRP, consistent with FMRP activating their translation. Of the other five, two are about the translation of FMR1's own mRNA, two describe FMRP repressing translation, and one says only that FMRP regulates a target's translation.

> Many genes encoding large proteins were translationally downregulated over a similar range (Fig. 1a), and the affected mRNAs had 3.4 times longer CDS lengths as compared to all cortex-expressed genes (4,797 vs 1,401 bp, respectively, Fig. 1b). **If FMRP acts directly to activate translation, then mRNAs bound by FMRP should be selectively reduced rather than increased in translation in mutant tissues.** Consistent with FMRP acting directly, mouse cortex mRNAs bound by FMRP had reduced ribosome footprints in Fmr1-null animals (Das Sharma et al. 2019).

— Flanagan K, Baradaran-Heravi A, Yin Q, Dao Duc K, Spradling AC, Greenblatt EJ (2022). FMRP-dependent production of large dosage-sensitive proteins is highly conserved. *Genetics*. [PMID:35731217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35731217/).


**Reasoning** (evidence-cited; verdict *acceptable, the gene acts both ways*, high confidence; cause: dropped term): FMR1's inherited 'positive regulation of translation' is backed by two of its own IDA papers, so it is not wrong, but FMR1 also has three IDA papers and two GO-CAMs for negative regulation of translation. In v1 FMR1 carried both directions from the same node, and the current release dropped the negative one. FMR1 acts both ways, so the problem is the dropped term, not the inherited one.

- *For:* FMR1 has two of its own IDA annotations (different papers) to positive regulation of translation, the inherited term. ([PMID:19097999](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19097999/); [PMID:19166269](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19166269/); FMR1)
- *Against:* FMR1 has three IDA annotations from different papers to negative regulation of translation, and two human GO-CAMs show FMR1 mRNA binding as part of translational repression in ribonucleoprotein granules. ([PMID:12417522](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12417522/); [PMID:30765518](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30765518/); [PMID:31439799](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31439799/); gomodel:63894f2500001337; gomodel:63894f2500001378)
- *Context:* In v1, FMR1 inherited negative regulation of translation from the same node PTN001318100 alongside the positive term; the negative term has since been dropped although the node still exists. (PAN-GO v1; PANTHER tree)
- *Context:* The paralog FXR1 has GO-CAMs showing positive regulation of translation, and the evidence set mixes orthologs, paralogs and FMR1 itself. (gomodel:63894f2500000870; gomodel:63894f2500000826; Fmr1; Fxr1; FXR1)
- *Context:* Reviews describe FMRP as controlling the translation of hundreds of specific mRNAs, consistent with target-dependent effects in either direction. (Salcedo-Arellano et al. 2020; Hagerman et al. 2017; Yoon and Bassell 2022)

*Reasoner's suggested fix:* Keep the positive regulation of translation IBA; restore the gain of 'negative regulation of translation' ([GO:0017148](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0017148)) at PTN001318100 or at the FMR1 clade, since FMR1's own IDA and GO-CAM evidence supports it.

**Suggested change:**

- Restore the gain of *negative regulation of translation* ([GO:0017148](https://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0017148)) at PTN001318100. FMR1's own experimental annotations support both directions, and v1 carried both. In v1 the gain reached FMR1, FXR1 and FXR2. Restoring it also gives the term to FXR1, whose own experimental annotations go the other way (3 annotations from 3 papers); and to FXR2, which has no experimental annotations about this. Check those genes before restoring it.
- Mouse Fxr1 was itself an evidence gene for the v1 gain. It has its own IDA annotations to negative regulation of translation ([PMID:25456134](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25456134/)) as well as to positive regulation ([PMID:35951695](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35951695/)). So FXR1 may act both ways, like FMR1, and a loss for FXR1 would contradict mouse Fxr1.
- Two papers argue against restoring the gain where it reaches FXR1 and FXR2. In Laggerbauer et al. 2001 ([PMID:11157796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11157796/)), the source of FMR1's translation-repressor annotation, FXR1 and FXR2 failed to suppress translation at the doses at which FMRP did. In Coffee et al. 2010 ([PMID:20442204](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20442204/)), a source of the v1 gain, human FMR1 rescued the fly Fmr1 null in neurons, but FXR1 and FXR2 did not. A gain at the vertebrate FMR1 clade (PTN002577677, Euteleostomi) would fit these papers better.

### References
- Birsa N, Ule AM, Garone MG, Tsang B, Mattedi F, Chong PA et al. (2021). FUS-ALS mutants alter FMRP phase separation equilibrium and impair protein translation. *Science advances*. [PMID:34290090](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34290090/).
- Coffee RL, Tessier CR, Woodruff EA, Broadie K (2010). Fragile X mental retardation protein has a unique, evolutionarily conserved neuronal function not shared with FXR1P or FXR2P. *Dis Model Mech*. [PMID:20442204](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20442204/).
- Flanagan K, Baradaran-Heravi A, Yin Q, Dao Duc K, Spradling AC, Greenblatt EJ (2022). FMRP-dependent production of large dosage-sensitive proteins is highly conserved. *Genetics*. [PMID:35731217](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35731217/).
- Hagerman RJ, Berry-Kravis E, Hazlett HC, Bailey DB, Moine H, Kooy RF et al. (2017). Fragile X syndrome. *Nat Rev Dis Primers*. [PMID:28960184](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28960184/).
- Laggerbauer B, Ostareck D, Keidel EM, Ostareck-Lederer A, Fischer U (2001). Evidence that fragile X mental retardation protein is a negative regulator of translation. *Hum Mol Genet*. [PMID:11157796](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11157796/).
- Salcedo-Arellano MJ, Hagerman RJ, Martínez-Cerdeño V (2020). Fragile X syndrome: clinical presentation, pathology and treatment. *Gac Med Mex*. [PMID:32026885](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32026885/).
- Yoon YJ, Bassell GJ (2022). Diversity on location. *Elife*. [PMID:35129438](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35129438/).
title: PAINT issue: PTHR10603: FMR1 lost "negative regulation of translation" and now only inherits "positive regulation of translation"
